entries.name: Integrated gradients
entries.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
entries.definition: A feature-attribution method that integrates a prediction's input gradients along the straight path from a chosen baseline to the input.
entries.mechanism: Each feature receives its input-minus-baseline difference multiplied by the integral of that feature's partial derivative along the path; the paper approximates the integral with a finite gradient sum.
entries.locator: Section 3, equation 1, PDF p. 3; Section 5, equation 3 and baseline selection, PDF pp. 5–6
entries.identity_notes: Straight-path gradient integration differs from a gradient at one input, layer-wise contribution propagation and Shapley averaging across feature orderings.
limitations: Attributions depend on the baseline; an arbitrary zero-score baseline need not give a meaningful absence of signal.
Numerical integration is approximate. This record makes no universal causal-faithfulness or superiority claim.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The authors use attribution axioms to design a method and demonstrate it on image, text and chemistry networks. Those examples do not establish universal explanation quality.
entries.mapping_rationale: The method attributes outputs of artificial neural networks to their inputs in the defining paper. This direct analysis relationship does not make the method a neural-network architecture.

entries.name: DeepLIFT
entries.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
entries.definition: A neural-network attribution method that distributes an output's difference from a reference activation to input differences using backward contribution propagation.
entries.mechanism: Reference inputs determine reference activations. Local contribution multipliers compose backward subject to summation-to-delta; Linear, Rescale and RevealCancel rules determine local allocation, with RevealCancel treating positive and negative differences separately.
entries.locator: Sections 3.1–3.5, equations 1–4 and Linear/Rescale/RevealCancel rules, PDF pp. 2–5
entries.identity_notes: This record covers the 2017 DeepLIFT method including distinct local rules; it is not identical to gradients, integrated gradients, Deep SHAP or the earlier Rescale-only formulation.
limitations: Reference and local-rule choices affect attribution. The paper discusses cases favoring Rescale or RevealCancel rather than one universally superior rule.
Contribution conservation is not a proof of causal feature importance or exact Shapley values for an arbitrary network.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The paper assigns contributions relative to reference activations and evaluates MNIST and simulated genomic tasks. Its reported advantages are conditional on those methods and evaluations.
entries.mapping_rationale: The defining method propagates contributions through an artificial neural network. The related mapping identifies that direct analysis object, not architecture identity or subclasshood.

entries.name: SmoothGrad
entries.title: SmoothGrad: removing noise by adding noise
entries.definition: A sensitivity-map smoothing method that averages maps computed on Gaussian-noise perturbations of an input.
entries.mechanism: Sample multiple noisy copies of the input, compute the selected sensitivity map on each, and average the maps to estimate a local smoothing of that map function.
entries.locator: Section 2.2, PDF pp. 2–3; unnumbered SmoothGrad averaging equation on p. 3
entries.identity_notes: SmoothGrad is an averaging wrapper around a sensitivity-map method, not a new trained network, a training-noise procedure or an exact equivalent of its underlying gradient map.
limitations: The result depends on the base map, noise scale and sample count.
The paper's visual-coherence comparisons and proposed explanation for noise do not establish universal attribution faithfulness.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The authors propose smoothing gradient-based sensitivity maps and discuss visualization choices. Visual sharpness is the central reported improvement, not a guarantee of causal interpretation.
entries.mapping_rationale: The defining method smooths sensitivity maps of artificial-neural-network outputs. This direct analysis relationship is not an assertion that SmoothGrad is itself a network.

entries.name: Layer-wise relevance propagation
entries.title: On Pixel-Wise Explanations for Non-Linear Classifier Decisions by Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation
entries.definition: A prediction-decomposition framework that redistributes relevance backward through a classifier's computational layers toward its input features.
entries.mechanism: Starting from an output score, layer-specific rules allocate relevance messages to preceding units and sum incoming messages until the input is reached. The neural-network procedure supplies stabilized and positive/negative contribution rules.
entries.locator: Layer-wise relevance propagation, equation 2, PDF/printed pp. 3–4; Layer-wise relevance backpropagation, equations 55–62 and Algorithm 2, pp. 20–21
entries.identity_notes: LRP is a family of constrained relevance-propagation constructions, demonstrated for neural networks and kernel-based Bag-of-Words classifiers; it is not a single gradient formula or a classifier-training algorithm.
limitations: Conservation alone does not uniquely determine meaningful attributions; the original paper gives a counterexample.
Bias terms and epsilon stabilization can absorb relevance, so exact conservation is not asserted for every practical rule.
entries.abstract_interpretation: The paper develops pixel-wise prediction decompositions for two classifier families and visualizes them as heatmaps. It analyzes existing classifiers rather than supplying a training method.
entries.mapping_rationale: The paper explicitly constructs LRP for artificial neural networks. This related mapping records that supported analysis relationship while retaining LRP's additional kernel-classifier scope; it asserts neither equivalence nor exclusive applicability.
